headline: West end flood: bonito nose into the Buzzards Bay side as east end bass eat the ebb
subhead: New moon current pushed 4.5-knot water through the ditch all week, and both ends are showing signs the fall pattern is locking in.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning the flood hit the east end wall around 6:50, running close to 4.5 knots by the time it topped out — that's about as much water as this canal moves on anything short of a full moon spring tide, and it's exactly what the September 10 new moon was supposed to deliver. We flagged this last week — said the bass would build on the tide changes as the moon strengthened the current, and that's precisely what's happened. The bunker got squeezed hard against both ends of the ditch this week, and the stripers committed the way they should when the water's moving like that.

Here's how the current's been working the two ends. On the east side, off the power plant and down toward the Herring Run, the last two hours of the ebb — water pulling east, back out toward Cape Cod Bay — has been the number one window. Bait gets pinned against the rocks and the rip line forms hard off the tip of the jetty, and that's where the bass have been sitting, facing into the current, letting the moving water do the work. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or olive, cast up-current and swung down through the seam, have been the go-to. Guys throwing white Storm swim shads on wider bucktail heads have done well too when the current's really cranking and you need weight to hold bottom contact. Bluefish are mixed right in with the bass on that same ebb — nothing giant, mostly 3 to 6 pounds, but enough of them that if you're not using wire or a heavy fluoro leader you're going to lose gear.

The west end has been the more interesting story this week. With the albie and bonito run stabilizing hard across Buzzards Bay — Cuttyhunk, the Elizabeth Islands side, up into Westport — that warm-water edge has been pushing bait right up against Wings Neck and into Phinneys Harbor, and it's only a matter of time before that pressure starts showing fish right at the Mass Maritime Academy seam and the Railroad Bridge rip. A few reports out of the west end this week had small showings of bonito working bait pods on the last of the flood, right where the current coming out of Buzzards Bay collides with the eddy off the Bourne side. It wasn't a full-blown blitz, more a tease — three or four fish seen, one or two hooked on 3/8-ounce Deadly Dicks and small Albie Snax — but that's the leading edge of a pattern that's been running strong to our east all week, and it should keep pushing this direction as the warm filament holds.

Stripers at the west end have been more reliable than the albies right now, and the timing is almost the mirror image of the east side — here it's the building flood, water pushing hard west into Buzzards Bay, that turns the bite on. Fish are stacking on the current seams below Mashnee Island and along the edge of the flats off Hog Island, ambushing bait getting funneled through on the push. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, dropped just off the seam and allowed to swing naturally with the current, have out-produced the plugs this week for the better fish — 28 to 34 inches, with a few pushing into the high 30s reported around the top of the flood. Topwater guys working Danny plugs and Gibbs Polaris poppers at first light before the current builds have had some fun with smaller schoolies too, though the bigger fish clearly want the moving water and the depth.

Fluke have mostly cleared out of the canal proper — that fishery's shifted out to Nantucket Sound and the Shoals for the better grade, which tracks with what's happening everywhere else on the Cape right now. If you're targeting fluke inside the ditch this week, expect mostly short fish working the sandy stretches on slower current near dead low, nothing worth writing home about.

Looking ahead: the moon's still close enough to new that the tides through the weekend should stay strong, current running 4 knots-plus on both ends near the max stages. That's good news for the east end bass-and-blue pattern, which should hold steady on the ebb through at least midweek. The bigger question is whether the west end albie showing turns into something real. If the Buzzards Bay warm edge keeps advancing the way it has across Rhode Island and the islands, the next few days are when we'd expect the first legitimate west end albie run of the fall — worth checking the Railroad Bridge rip and the water off Mashnee on the last hour of the flood, right where the bait's getting squeezed against the seam. If that edge stalls or slides back east toward the islands instead, the west end sticks with the striper pattern on eels and bucktails, which isn't a bad consolation prize. Either way, the current's doing the heavy lifting right now — read the clock, work the last two hours of whichever tide is running on your end, and don't fight the water.
